confusables.howToTell: Palpation is what your hands do during the exam; palpitations are what the patient's heart does. One extra syllable, a completely different chart note.
confusables.exampleA: On palpation, the liver edge was two centimeters below the costal margin.
confusables.exampleB: She reports palpitations whenever she climbs the dormitory stairs.

confusables.howToTell: The ilEum is the last part of the small intestine (E for Eat); the ilIum is the flaring hip bone (I for hIp). Same sound, opposite ends of the body.
confusables.exampleA: The terminal ileum is the classic site for Crohn's disease.
confusables.exampleB: The needle for the marrow biopsy went into the iliac crest of the ilium.

confusables.howToTell: Mucus (noun) is the slippery stuff; mucous (adjective) describes the membrane that makes it. The noun has the 'us' you can blow into a tissue.
confusables.exampleA: Thick green mucus was pouring from the sinuses.
confusables.exampleB: The mucous membranes were dry, suggesting she was dehydrated.

confusables.howToTell: Perfusion is blood flow through a tissue; profusion is a great abundance of something. A profusion of bleeding is very bad for perfusion.
confusables.exampleA: Cold, mottled feet warned us that distal perfusion was failing.
confusables.exampleB: He apologized with such profusion that it became awkward.

confusables.howToTell: DysphaGia is trouble swallowing (G as in Gulp/Gut); dysphaSia is trouble with speech/language (S as in Speech). One letter sends the workup to a different specialty.
confusables.exampleA: Progressive dysphagia for solids prompted an urgent endoscopy.
confusables.exampleB: After the stroke he had an expressive dysphasia and struggled to find words.

confusables.howToTell: Aural relates to the ear (think 'audio'); oral relates to the mouth. An aural exam looks in the ear, an oral exam looks in the mouth.
confusables.exampleA: Aural discharge and pain pointed to an ear infection.
confusables.exampleB: The medication is taken by the oral route, twice a day.

confusables.howToTell: Vesical (adjective) relates to the bladder; a vesicle (noun) is a small fluid-filled skin blister. The bladder one ends in '-al' like an adjective should.
confusables.exampleA: Vesical tenesmus is a painful, persistent urge to empty the bladder.
confusables.exampleB: Clustered vesicles in a dermatomal band suggested shingles.

confusables.howToTell: Peroneal refers to the outer lower leg and its nerve; perineal refers to the region between the genitals and anus. (The unrelated 'peritoneal' is the abdominal lining — a third trap entirely.)
confusables.exampleA: A peroneal nerve palsy gave him a classic foot drop.
confusables.exampleB: Perineal soreness after delivery is common and usually settles quickly.

confusables.howToTell: To enervate is to drain of energy and weaken; to innervate is to supply a part with nerves. They're near-opposites despite looking like twins.
confusables.exampleA: The relentless heat enervated the whole team by midafternoon.
confusables.exampleB: The median nerve innervates most of the muscles of the thenar eminence.

confusables.howToTell: The prostate is the gland (no second R); to be prostrate is to lie face-down or be overcome (with the extra R, as in 'sprawled'). Examiners love this one.
confusables.exampleA: A digital rectal exam assessed the size of the prostate.
confusables.exampleB: He was found prostrate on the bathroom floor after the collapse.

confusables.howToTell: A callus (noun) is hardened skin or healing bone; callous (adjective) means emotionally hardened and unfeeling. The skin one is the noun.
confusables.exampleA: A thick callus had built up over the old fracture site.
confusables.exampleB: His callous remark about the diagnosis upset the whole family.

confusables.howToTell: Discreet (double-e in the middle) means tactful and private; discrete means separate and distinct. The two e's of 'discreet' hide together, keeping a secret.
confusables.exampleA: Please be discreet about the diagnosis until she's ready to tell people.
confusables.exampleB: The rash consisted of discrete lesions that didn't merge together.

confusables.howToTell: Principal (with -pal) means main, or the head person — your 'pal' the boss; principle (with -ple) is a rule or belief. The main diagnosis is the principal one.
confusables.exampleA: The principal concern is the bleeding, not the mildly abnormal sodium.
confusables.exampleB: Respect for patient autonomy is a core ethical principle.

confusables.howToTell: Usually affect is the verb (to influence) and effect is the noun (the result). In psychiatry, 'affect' is also a noun meaning observed emotional expression.
confusables.exampleA: The new dose didn't noticeably affect her blood pressure.
confusables.exampleB: We're still waiting to see the full effect of the antibiotics.

confusables.howToTell: To elicit (verb) is to draw out a response or sign; illicit (adjective) means illegal. You elicit a reflex; you ask tactfully about illicit drug use.
confusables.exampleA: I couldn't elicit any tenderness even on deep palpation.
confusables.exampleB: The history screens for both prescribed and illicit substances.

confusables.howToTell: Adverse means harmful or unfavorable (an adverse reaction); averse means having a strong dislike (averse to risk). A drug has adverse effects; a person is averse to taking it.
confusables.exampleA: We documented the adverse reaction to penicillin in her allergy list.
confusables.exampleB: He's deeply averse to needles, so we used the cream first.

confusables.howToTell: Eminent means distinguished and respected; imminent means about to happen at any moment. The eminent professor warned that collapse was imminent.
confusables.exampleA: The lecture was given by an eminent professor of immunology.
confusables.exampleB: Falling oxygen levels signaled that respiratory failure was imminent.

confusables.howToTell: Complement (with an E) completes or pairs with something; a compliment (with an I) is praise. The wine complements the meal; the chef appreciates a compliment.
confusables.exampleA: Imaging complements the blood tests rather than replacing them.
confusables.exampleB: She paid the junior doctor a genuine compliment on the round.

confusables.howToTell: Ensure means to make certain; insure means to arrange financial cover against loss. (The third sibling, assure, means to reassure a person.)
confusables.exampleA: Double-check the dose to ensure it's safe before you sign.
confusables.exampleB: The clinic had to insure its expensive new scanner against damage.

confusables.howToTell: To flaunt is to show off; to flout is to openly disregard a rule. People flaunt their wealth and flout the law — never the other way around.
confusables.exampleA: He flaunted his exam results to anyone who'd listen.
confusables.exampleB: Repeatedly flouting the hand-hygiene policy put patients at risk.

confusables.howToTell: The speaker implies (hints); the listener infers (deduces). If I imply something, you infer it. They travel in opposite directions.
confusables.exampleA: From her guarded answers I inferred that something was wrong at home.
confusables.exampleB: I didn't say it was your fault — I didn't even imply it.

confusables.howToTell: Continual means repeated with breaks (continual interruptions); continuous means unbroken (a continuous infusion). One stutters, the other never stops.
confusables.exampleA: Continual interruptions made the ward round take twice as long.
confusables.exampleB: She was on a continuous insulin infusion overnight.

confusables.howToTell: Historic means famous or important in history; historical simply means relating to the past. A historic decision changed medicine; a historical detail is just old.
confusables.exampleA: The first transplant was a historic moment for the field.
confusables.exampleB: Her historical notes from a decade ago held the missing clue.

confusables.howToTell: Fortuitous strictly means happening by chance; fortunate means lucky. A chance event can be fortuitous without being fortunate — though the two often overlap.
confusables.exampleA: It was entirely fortuitous that the cardiologist happened to be passing.
confusables.exampleB: We were fortunate that the bleeding stopped on its own.

confusables.howToTell: Disinterested means impartial, with no stake in the outcome; uninterested means bored, not caring. You want a disinterested judge, not an uninterested one.
confusables.exampleA: An ethics committee should give disinterested, unbiased advice.
confusables.exampleB: He seemed completely uninterested in the lecture and kept checking his phone.

confusables.howToTell: A regimen is a planned course of treatment or routine; a regiment is a military unit. Patients follow a drug regimen, not a drug regiment.
confusables.exampleA: The new chemotherapy regimen is given over three-week cycles.
confusables.exampleB: His grandfather served in an infantry regiment during the war.

confusables.howToTell: A dose is a single specified amount; dosage is the regulated pattern of doses over time. You give one dose; you adjust the overall dosage.
confusables.exampleA: Give a single 500-milligram dose now.
confusables.exampleB: We reviewed the dosage — frequency and duration — at the follow-up.

confusables.howToTell: Aseptic means free from contamination (an aseptic technique keeps germs out); an antiseptic is a substance that kills germs on living tissue. (The related 'septic' means infected.)
confusables.exampleA: The line was placed under strict aseptic technique.
confusables.exampleB: She cleaned the wound with an antiseptic solution before dressing it.

confusables.howToTell: A perspective is a point of view; prospective means relating to the future or expected. A prospective study looks forward; a fresh perspective looks differently.
confusables.exampleA: The patient's perspective on quality of life shaped the whole plan.
confusables.exampleB: A prospective trial will follow new patients forward in time.

confusables.howToTell: Than makes comparisons (bigger than); then marks time or sequence (and then). If you're comparing, it's the one with an 'a'.
confusables.exampleA: The second dose was better tolerated than the first.
confusables.exampleB: Examine the patient first, then write the note.

confusables.howToTell: The whole comprises the parts (no 'of'); the parts compose the whole. 'Is comprised of' is technically frowned upon — use 'comprises' or 'is composed of'.
confusables.exampleA: The nephron comprises the glomerulus and the tubule.
confusables.exampleB: Several distinct cell types compose the alveolar wall.

confusables.howToTell: Viscous (adjective) means thick and sticky, like syrup; viscera (noun) are the internal organs. Bile is viscous; the liver is one of the viscera.
confusables.exampleA: The aspirated fluid was thick and viscous.
confusables.exampleB: Blunt trauma can injure the abdominal viscera without breaking the skin.

confusables.howToTell: An apophysis is a bony outgrowth where a tendon attaches; an epiphysis is the end of a long bone that ossifies separately. Both are growth zones, but only the epiphysis forms a joint surface.
confusables.exampleA: The tibial apophysis is the sore bump in Osgood-Schlatter disease.
confusables.exampleB: A fracture through the epiphysis can disturb future bone growth.

confusables.howToTell: Hyper- means too much or above; hypo- means too little or below. Hyperkalemia is high potassium, hypokalemia is low — and mixing them up can be fatal.
confusables.exampleA: Hyperkalemia can stop the heart and shows peaked T waves on the ECG.
confusables.exampleB: Hypokalemia from vomiting left her weak and crampy.

confusables.howToTell: Tortuous means full of twists and bends; torturous means causing torture or agony. A tortuous artery winds; a torturous night drags painfully on.
confusables.exampleA: The angiogram showed a tortuous, corkscrew coronary artery.
confusables.exampleB: The wait for the biopsy result felt absolutely torturous.

confusables.howToTell: The perineum is the external area between the genitals and anus; the peritoneum is the membrane lining the abdominal cavity. Two extra letters move you deep inside the belly.
confusables.exampleA: The perineum was examined after a prolonged delivery.
confusables.exampleB: Free air under the diaphragm meant the peritoneum had been breached.

confusables.howToTell: The metaphysis is the growing region of a long bone near the ends; a metastasis is a cancer deposit that has spread. Similar opening, wildly different meaning.
confusables.exampleA: Osteomyelitis in children often starts in the metaphysis.
confusables.exampleB: A solitary lung metastasis was found on the staging scan.

confusables.howToTell: Lightening means becoming lighter (and in obstetrics, the baby dropping into the pelvis); lightning is the electrical flash. The obstetric one keeps the middle 'e'.
confusables.exampleA: Lightening in late pregnancy is the sensation of the baby settling lower.
confusables.exampleB: The power went out when lightning struck near the hospital.

confusables.howToTell: Anuresis (like anuria) is failure to produce or pass urine; enuresis is involuntary urination, classically bedwetting. One is too little urine, the other is poor control.
confusables.exampleA: Post-operative anuresis prompted an urgent bladder scan.
confusables.exampleB: Nocturnal enuresis in children usually resolves with time.

confusables.howToTell: To perfuse (verb) is to push fluid through a tissue; profuse (adjective) means abundant or copious. Profuse sweating is a symptom; perfusing an organ keeps it alive.
confusables.exampleA: The surgeons perfused the donor kidney before transplanting it.
confusables.exampleB: He arrived with profuse sweating and a racing pulse.

confusables.howToTell: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline (think 'abduct' = take away); adduction brings it back toward the midline (think 'add' to the body). One letter flips the direction.
confusables.exampleA: Shoulder abduction was limited to ninety degrees by the pain.
confusables.exampleB: Weak hip adduction made it hard for her to keep her knees together.

confusables.howToTell: Afferent fibers arrive at a center (A for Arrive/toward); efferent fibers exit toward the periphery (E for Exit). Sensory nerves are afferent, motor nerves efferent.
confusables.exampleA: Afferent signals from the skin travel toward the spinal cord.
confusables.exampleB: Efferent motor fibers carry the command out to the muscle.

confusables.howToTell: Psychosis is a severe mental state with loss of contact with reality; sycosis is a chronic inflammation of hair follicles. Identical sound, but only one is a dermatology diagnosis.
confusables.exampleA: Acute psychosis with paranoid delusions prompted urgent assessment.
confusables.exampleB: Sycosis barbae is a stubborn folliculitis of the beard area.

confusables.howToTell: Mucous is the adjective (mucous membrane); the mucosa is the noun for that lining itself. You examine the mucosa, which is the mucous membrane.
confusables.exampleA: The buccal mucous membrane looked dry and cracked.
confusables.exampleB: Endoscopy showed an inflamed, friable gastric mucosa.

confusables.howToTell: The humerus is the upper arm bone; humorous means funny. The bone has the 'e'; the joke has the 'o'. The 'funny bone' pun is the eternal trap.
confusables.exampleA: He fractured the surgical neck of the humerus in the fall.
confusables.exampleB: Her humorous bedside manner put nervous patients at ease.
